title: Labeling and discriminating a /b/ to /d/ to /g/ continuum
asked: Are speech sounds heard in proportion to their acoustic differences, or by category?
did: They used the pattern playback synthesizer to make syllables whose F2 transition changed in equal steps. Listeners labeled each sound as /b/, /d/ or /g/ and judged whether pairs were the same or different.
found: Labels switched sharply over a step or two. Discrimination **peaked** at the category boundaries and was near chance inside categories.
means: Equal physical steps are heard very differently depending on whether they cross a boundary. This is **categorical perception**.

title: Four-month-olds and voice onset time
asked: Do infants hear voice onset time categorically before they can talk?
did: Four-month-olds heard one syllable through high amplitude sucking until sucking dropped. In 20D, VOT then changed by 20 ms across an adult boundary. In 20S, it changed by 20 ms within one category, and a control group heard no change.
found: Sucking **recovered** after the 20D change. It kept falling after the 20S change, much like the control.
means: Infants perceive VOT categorically very early. That seemed like evidence that a language-specific ability is innate.

title: Losing non-native contrasts in the first year
asked: How do age and language experience affect infants’ ability to hear contrasts their language does not use?
did: They tested English-learning infants at three ages from 6 to 12 months. The contrasts were a Hindi Ta/ta contrast and a Salish ki/qi contrast. Hindi-learning and Salish-learning infants were tested too.
found: Most English-learning infants discriminated both contrasts at 6 to 8 months, and very few did at 10 to 12 months. Infants learning Hindi or Salish kept their own contrast.
means: Perception narrows toward the native language during the first year. This is **perceptual narrowing**, and it depends on experience.

title: Categorical perception of plucked and bowed sounds
asked: Is categorical perception limited to speech?
did: Listeners labeled sawtooth sounds that varied in rise time as pluck or bow, and discriminated pairs along the continuum.
found: The labels switched over a narrow range. Discrimination **peaked** right at that switch.
means: Categorical perception appears for sounds that are not language, so it is not special to the language system.

title: Infants and non-speech categories
asked: Do infants also perceive non-speech sounds categorically?
did: Infants heard a non-speech sound through high amplitude sucking until sucking dropped. The sound then stayed the same, changed within a category, or changed between categories.
found: Sucking jumped back up only after a change between categories.
means: Infants respond categorically to non-speech sounds too. So their categorical response to speech may come from general auditory processing.

title: Chinchillas categorize a speech continuum
asked: Do animals without language perceive speech sounds categorically, as Kuhl and Miller (1975) had suggested?
did: Chinchillas were trained with operant conditioning that either the 0 ms lag or the 80 ms lag sound signaled food. They were then tested on sounds along the /ga/ to /ka/ continuum.
found: The chinchillas switched over a narrow range of VOTs. Their curves had the same steep shape as human curves.
means: Categorical perception of speech is not limited to humans.

title: Some contrasts need exposure to become salient
asked: Are all speech contrasts equally easy for young infants?
did: They compared infants’ looking on same and change trials for /ma/ versus /na/ and for /na/ versus /ŋa/. They tested English-hearing infants and Filipino-learning infants at different ages.
found: Four-month-olds noticed /ma/ versus /na/ but not /na/ versus /ŋa/. Filipino-learning infants missed /na/ versus /ŋa/ at 6 to 8 months but detected it by 10 to 12 months.
means: Not all contrasts are available innately. Exposure is necessary to acquire some of them.

title: Learning categories from a distribution
asked: Do infants learn speech categories from the statistics of what they hear?
did: Infants listened passively to a [da] to [ta] VOT continuum in either a bimodal distribution, with two peaks, or a unimodal one, with one peak. At test they heard stimuli 3 and 6 in alternating or non-alternating trials.
found: Only infants exposed to the bimodal distribution looked differently on the two kinds of trials.
means: Unimodal infants acted as if 3 and 6 were one category. So a short exposure to a distribution shapes speech categories.

title: Social interaction in learning speech sounds
asked: Does social interaction matter for learning speech sounds?
did: Nine-month-old American infants were exposed to Mandarin live, by video or by audio, and then tested on a Mandarin contrast. In another study, mothers of eight-month-olds responded either right after the infant vocalized or on an unrelated schedule.
found: Only live exposure produced learning of the Mandarin contrast. Contingent responses increased the quantity and complexity of infants’ vocalizations.
means: Social interaction works much like a reinforcing stimulus. Humans may find it innately rewarding or be innately good at using social cues.

title: Gradient competition between bear and pear
asked: Is phoneme identification for word recognition thresholded or cascaded?
did: Listeners heard words from a /b/ to /p/ VOT continuum and clicked a bear or pear image in a visual world display. Their eye movements were tracked.
found: Clicks gave a step-like identification curve. But looks to the competitor rose gradually as VOT neared the boundary, even when the final click was the same.
means: Ambiguity is gradient, so graded feature activation reaches the word level. This supports **cascaded** processing.

title: Semantic priming from nonwords
asked: Can partial or imperfect input activate words and their meanings?
did: Primes had the voicing of their first consonant altered, so “peace” became “beace” and “king” became “ging.” Priming of related targets was measured with lexical decision.
found: “Beace” primed “war,” and “ging” primed “queen.”
means: Lexical representations can be activated by incomplete input, which fits cascaded processing.

title: Word knowledge shifts phoneme boundaries
asked: Is phoneme identification affected by word knowledge?
did: He built continua in 5 ms steps between a word and a nonword, such as corpse and gorpse. Listeners labeled the first sound.
found: The lexical effect was small at the endpoints and largest near the category boundary.
means: Word knowledge shifts the category boundary itself rather than adding a late reporting bias. Later models explain this with **feedback** from words to phonemes.

title: The cohort effect in spoken word recognition
asked: How quickly do candidate words become active as a spoken word unfolds?
did: Listeners followed spoken instructions such as moving the beaker while viewing a beaker, a beetle, a speaker and a carriage. Eye movements were tracked.
found: Looks to the beaker and the cohort competitor beetle rose together at first. Looks to the rhyme competitor speaker came later and stayed smaller.
means: Words that match the input so far compete as soon as the word begins. TRACE simulations closely match this time course.

title: An apple, a towel and a box
asked: Can the visual scene change how a spoken sentence is parsed?
did: People saw a display and heard “Put the apple on the towel in the box.” The display had either one apple, sitting on a towel, or two apples, only one on a towel.
found: With one apple, people looked at the empty towel as if it were the destination. With two apples, they looked at it much less.
means: Different parses of the same sentence are favored in different contexts, very early. This is a big problem for purely syntactic accounts.

title: Mouse paths in the apple and towel task
asked: Does syntactic ambiguity affect the action itself, not just eye movements?
did: Participants carried out the apple and towel instructions with a computer mouse while its path was tracked.
found: With one apple, the hand curved toward the empty towel on ambiguous instructions. With two apples, ambiguous and unambiguous paths were nearly the same.
means: Syntactic ambiguity and visual context influence the actual execution of arm movements.

title: Early visual responses and form typicality
asked: Is the earliest response to a word category violation based on abstract syntax or on the word’s physical form?
did: Readers saw an adjective or an adverb followed by a noun, as in “The beautiful princess” versus “The beautifully princess.” Nouns had a noun suffix, a typical noun form, or neither, as in infant.
found: The unexpected version produced a larger early visual response only for nouns with a suffix or a noun-like form. Neutral nouns like infant showed no effect.
means: The earliest syntactic effect comes from visual cortex and depends on predicted word forms.

title: Broca’s patients and reversible sentences
asked: Do Broca’s patients have a comprehension deficit for syntax, or only a motor problem in speaking?
did: Patients and controls did a sentence-picture matching task with control, semantically constrained, reversible and improbable center-embedded sentences.
found: Controls did well on all types, and Wernicke’s patients were poor overall. Broca’s patients failed mainly when syntax conflicted with common sense.
means: This specific deficit was taken as evidence that Broca’s aphasia affects syntax specifically.

title: Sentence types, aphasia and stressed listeners
asked: Is the Broca’s pattern a loss of grammar or a processing limit?
did: Participants heard active, subject cleft, object cleft and passive sentences and indicated which animal did the action. Aphasic patients, elderly controls and stressed undergraduates were tested.
found: Broca’s patients had particular difficulty with object clefts and passives and were weak overall. Undergraduates under speeded speech or memory load showed the same vulnerability.
means: The comprehension deficit in Broca’s aphasia may be a performance issue after all.

title: Actions and sounds without words
asked: Are aphasic comprehension deficits specific to language?
did: Patients matched actions to objects, given in words or by pantomime. They also matched environmental sounds or spoken phrases to pictures.
found: Broca’s aphasics had difficulty with actions whether or not the stimuli were linguistic, and this correlated with damage to Broca’s area. Wernicke’s patients were particularly bad at sound matching in both versions.
means: Damage to these areas affects meaning beyond language, so the deficits are not purely language-specific.

who: Bates, Wilson, Saygin, Dick, Sereno, Knight and Dronkers
title: Voxel-based lesion-symptom mapping
asked: Across many patients, which brain regions go with fluency and comprehension deficits?
did: They compared symptom scores at every voxel between patients with and without damage there, using MRI data.
found: Fluency deficits were linked to anterior regions. Comprehension deficits were linked to posterior regions.
means: Data from many patients fit a rough double dissociation between production and perception.

title: Stress as a cue to word beginnings
asked: Can infants use stress to find words in fluent speech?
did: Infants aged 7.5 months were familiarized with “kingdom” or “device” and then heard passages containing each word.
found: Infants familiarized with kingdom preferred the kingdom passage. Infants familiarized with device did not show that preference.
means: Most English words are stressed on the first syllable, so stress may help signal the beginnings of words.

title: Finding words by transitional probability
asked: Can infants find words using only transitional probabilities between syllables?
did: Infants heard a continuous, monotone stream of CV syllables made of three-syllable words such as tokibu. At test, words were compared with part-words matched for frequency.
found: Infants looked longer at part-words, a novelty effect.
means: Infants learned the statistical regularities of the stream, not just how often sequences occurred.

title: Joint attention and new words
asked: Does joint attention help infants learn word meanings?
did: An adult interacting with 18-month-olds labeled the object they were playing with, or a voice from behind a screen gave the label.
found: Infants learned the new word in the joint attention group but not in the no joint attention group.
means: Hearing a word near an object is not enough. Infants need evidence of the speaker’s intended referent.

title: Follow-in and discrepant labeling
asked: Do infants use the speaker’s eye gaze to decide what a new word means?
did: Infants aged 16 to 17 and 18 to 19 months were taught new words. In follow-in labeling, the adult looked at the toy the infant was focused on. In discrepant labeling, the adult looked at a toy in a bucket.
found: The two conditions pulled the infant’s focus apart from the speaker’s focus.
means: Gaze direction is an intentional cue that can narrow the hypothesis space for new words.

title: Facial expressions and word reference
asked: Do infants use emotional cues to find the referent of a new word?
did: Adults reacted with different facial expressions to objects while a new word was used.
found: Infants used the adults’ facial expressions to identify the intended referent.
means: Intention is conveyed through affective and behavioral cues, not only gaze.

title: Two-year-olds and a made-up verb
asked: Have young children learned the transitive structure itself?
did: Two-year-olds heard “The duck is gorping the bunny” while viewing a duck acting on a bunny and a bunny acting on a duck.
found: Children looked significantly longer at the duck acting on the bunny.
means: Children who say only short utterances can use transitive word order with a new verb.

title: Adult plasticity in amblyopia
asked: Is plasticity in the visual system gone after the critical period?
did: Adults with amblyopia, some in their 50s, trained intensively on psychophysical tasks with the affected eye.
found: Their task performance and general visual function improved.
means: Plasticity is not abolished in adulthood, so amblyopia fits a sensitive period.

who: Li, Ngo, Nguyen, Lam and Levi (2008)
title: Video games and adult amblyopia
asked: Can an engaging visual task improve vision in adult amblyopia?
did: Adults with amblyopia played action video games with the amblyopic eye.
found: Visual acuity and visual attention improved.
means: The right kind of experience can reverse deficits late into adulthood.

title: Genie
asked: What happens when a first language is learned only after puberty?
did: They studied Genie, isolated from 20 months of age and punished for making sounds until she was found at 13. Her language was observed for four years.
found: She came to understand hundreds of words, some morphology and some prepositions. Her production lagged far behind, and her grammar grew much more slowly than her vocabulary.
means: The gap between vocabulary and grammar is widely read as evidence that grammar learning is impaired after a sensitive period.

title: Late first language in deaf children
asked: Does the timing of a first language matter when upbringing is otherwise typical?
did: They studied deaf people who first learned ASL at ages 9 to 15 as their first language. They compared them with deaf people who had learned a spoken language before going deaf.
found: Those with no early language had much more difficulty, and the difference persisted into adulthood.
means: Having an early language, of any kind, matters for later learning, and deprivation does not extend the critical period.

title: Cognates in paired-associate learning
asked: Do people use cognates when learning second language words?
did: Dutch speakers learned made-up words paired with Dutch words that varied in cognate status and concreteness. They were tested productively and receptively and again a week later.
found: Cognates were learned more rapidly and remembered more easily. The advantage held in productive testing.
means: Cognate status contributes to the very earliest stages of second language word learning.

title: Cross-language competitors
asked: Are similar L1 words always activated when bilinguals process L2?
did: Russian and English bilinguals followed spoken instructions in English, then in Russian, while viewing objects. Some objects had names in the other language that began like the target, such as matches, spichki, for speaker.
found: In English, the Russian competitor drew looks about twice as often as a control. In Russian, the English competitor did not reliably draw looks.
means: L1 words are active during L2 listening, but not the reverse. The competition is asymmetric.

title: Korean adoptees and the Korean stop contrast
asked: Do adults adopted from Korea keep any ability to hear Korean stop contrasts?
did: Korean adoptees in France, French speakers and Korean speakers judged pairs of Korean stops, vowels and identical sounds.
found: Adoptees were no better than French speakers on the Korean stop contrasts, while all groups did well on vowels.
means: The early exposure to Korean left no detectable advantage in hearing its sounds.

title: Can a second language replace the first?
asked: Do Korean adoptees raised in French homes keep any trace of Korean?
did: Adults adopted at 3 to 8 years were tested on recognizing Korean, choosing Korean translations and detecting repeated excerpts. Their brain responses to French and to foreign languages were also imaged.
found: Adoptees were no better than French speakers on any task. Their brains treated Korean like other foreign languages.
means: When L1 is removed entirely, L2 can appear to replace it completely.

title: Childhood overhearers of Spanish
asked: Does overhearing a language in childhood leave traces that later learning can unmask?
did: Students who overheard Spanish as children but never spoke it took Spanish from about age 14. They were compared with native speakers and typical late learners after second-year college Spanish.
found: Overhearers had more native-like VOT and accents than late learners. They had little or no advantage in grammar.
means: Replacement of an early language may not be complete, at least for pronunciation.

title: Age of arrival and English grammar
asked: Does the critical period extend to second language learning?
did: They gave an untimed grammaticality judgment test to 46 native Korean or Chinese speakers who arrived in the United States between ages 3 and 39.
found: Scores fell with age of arrival up to puberty, and early learners up to about 8 were native-like. After puberty, scores were low and nearly random with respect to age of arrival.
means: They argued for a critical period that extends to L2, best fit by the **maturational state hypothesis**.

title: Implicit and explicit knowledge in grammar tests
asked: Does an untimed grammaticality judgment test measure grammar acquisition or explicit knowledge?
did: He compared tests that differ in time pressure and in whether they allow metalinguistic knowledge. He related scores to starting age and years of formal instruction.
found: Untimed GJT scores were correlated with years of formal L2 education. Starting age was related to the timed GJT.
means: An untimed GJT may measure **explicit** metalinguistic knowledge more than **implicit** grammar.

title: Changing the language pairing
asked: Does the age pattern depend on the learners’ first language?
did: They repeated the Johnson and Newport study with Spanish speakers learning English.
found: Early arrivals scored near the top regardless of age, and late arrivals declined steadily with age. This is almost the reverse of the Chinese and Korean pattern.
means: Age of arrival effects on the GJT depend on the language pairing, not only on maturation.
